title: Two quakes, one minute
subtitle: Venezuela earthquakes, June 2026

technical.title: Coseismic LOS displacement, northern Venezuela
technical.subtitle: ARIA map from NISAR L-band InSAR, 2026-06-24 M7.2 and M7.5
technical.summary: Coseismic LOS displacement from NASA JPL's ARIA map of a NISAR L-band (λ = 24.2 cm) interferogram, 12-day baseline (2026-06-13 to 06-25) spanning the M7.2 and M7.5 events (USGS). Unwrapped, ionosphere-corrected, deramped and water-masked; shown in meters (source in cm). LOS is relative to an unknown reference, so one geometry cannot separate vertical from horizontal.
caveats: The ARIA map is not yet validated by NASA and is guidance only. It may be less reliable over snow and vegetation.
LOS values are relative to an unknown reference level, so absolute offsets are not meaningful.

Left-looking ascending geometry, about 40 degrees from vertical toward the west-southwest. Positive = away from the satellite is inferred from NASA's description. NASA notes the motion was mostly horizontal.
Measurement coverage is derived by Aevion (share of valid cells in a 7 by 7 window). It is not interferometric coherence.
Exported at about 590 m per cell from a 30 m source, so fine detail is lost.

dataStatusNote: Ground motion is NASA JPL's ARIA line-of-sight displacement map made from the NISAR pair (not yet validated by NASA, relative to an unknown reference). The coverage layer is derived by Aevion from where that map has valid data. Earthquakes are from USGS and NISAR pass dates from NASA CMR.

statusDetail.story: NASA JPL ground-motion map from NISAR, not yet validated
statusDetail.scientist: ARIA LOS map (NISAR GUNW pair), not yet validated; coverage derived by Aevion

storyText: On June 24, 2026, a magnitude 7.2 and a magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck northern Venezuela within a minute of each other. NISAR flew over on June 13 and again on June 25. NASA's JPL compared those two radar passes to measure how far the ground moved along the satellite's line of sight, and this is their map.

geometry.source: NASA description of the ARIA map: about 40 degrees from vertical, slightly south of due west (ascending, left-looking)

why.title: Why did the ground move?
why.body: Northern Venezuela sits where the Caribbean and South American plates slide past each other, mostly sideways. Strain builds slowly and then releases. On June 24 two faults slipped within a minute. USGS finds both were right-lateral strike-slip on roughly east-west faults: one side slid to the right relative to the other, by up to about 1.8 m in USGS's model of the larger quake.

why.title: How does radar see the ground move?
why.body: NISAR sends L-band radar pulses (about 24 cm wavelength) and records the echo. Comparing two passes 12 days apart, a tiny change in the distance to the ground shifts the echo's phase. One full color cycle in the Fringes view is about 12 cm of motion. Radar works at night and through clouds.

why.title: What do polarizations add?
why.body: This map uses HH: the radar sends and receives horizontally polarized waves. Co-polarized channels like HH keep their phase well, which is why interferograms use them. Cross-polarized channels such as HV respond more to vegetation structure, so they suit forest and fire change more than ground motion.

why.title: What can the map not tell us?
why.body: The radar only measures motion along its line of sight, toward or away from the satellite, so one pass cannot separate up, down, east and west. The map is relative to an unknown reference and NASA has not yet validated it. Near the fault, shaking scrambles the radar echo, so some areas have no data.

why.title: What could NISAR do next?
why.body: NISAR images nearly all land every 12 days, so the same method can track landslides after storms, volcano swelling, sinking cities, moving glaciers, floods, and forest or crop change. NISAR also has urgent-response data products for disasters like this one.

tour.title: Northern Venezuela
tour.text: This is the coast of northern Venezuela, home to millions of people. Radar from space can measure how the ground moves here, even through clouds.

tour.title: NISAR looks once
tour.text: On June 13, NISAR, a NASA-ISRO radar satellite, passed over and recorded the ground. This is the 'before' picture.

tour.title: Two big earthquakes
tour.text: On June 24, a magnitude 7.2 and a magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck within a minute of each other. The beach balls show how the rock slipped: sideways, along east-west faults.

tour.title: NISAR looks again
tour.text: On June 25, NISAR flew over again. Comparing the two passes shows how the ground moved. Orange means away from the satellite, blue means toward it.

tour.title: The ground slid sideways
tour.text: South of the fault the ground moved one way, north of it the other. That is what sideways slip looks like. The purple patches are USGS's model of where the fault slipped.

tour.title: Counting the waves
tour.text: Each color band is about 12 cm of motion toward or away from the satellite. Many tight bands mean a lot of movement.

tour.title: How sure are we?
tour.text: Dark areas have gaps in the data, often where shaking or vegetation scrambled the radar. We hide what we cannot trust.

tour.title: Who felt it
tour.text: Cities along the coast felt violent shaking. USGS estimates millions of people were exposed to very strong shaking.

layers.name: Ground motion (line of sight)
layers.hintStory: Orange means the ground moved away from the satellite, blue means toward it. The satellite looks west-southwest, so orange is roughly westward motion.
layers.hintScientist: LOS displacement in meters. Positive = range increase (away from the satellite), per NASA's description and the left-looking ascending geometry. Relative to an unknown reference.

provenance.product: ARIA line-of-sight displacement map, derived from a NISAR L2 GUNW interferogram
provenance.producedBy: NASA JPL / Caltech ARIA team, NISAR Operations Science Team
provenance.service: NASA Disasters Mapping Portal image service (public)
provenance.maturity: PROVISIONAL (source GUNW); the map itself is not yet validated
provenance.measurement: Radar line-of-sight displacement, relative to an unknown reference level
provenance.signConvention: Positive = away from the satellite. NASA: red = toward the west, blue = toward the east. The satellite looks west-southwest (ascending, left-looking), so westward is away. Inferred; not independently verified.
provenance.geometry: Track 162 ascending, left-looking, frame 006 (and 007), HH, about 40 degrees from vertical, 80 m posting, EPSG:32619 (verified in the downloaded granule)
provenance.wavelength: 0.242 m (center frequency 1.239 GHz, read from the granule)
provenance.rawGranuleCheck: The raw granule (frame 006, about 7.6 to 10.2 N) was downloaded and opens correctly. It lies mostly south of the ruptures, where the ARIA signal is only a few cm, so it could not validate the map's amplitude or sign.
provenance.method: Unwrapped, ionosphere removed, deramped, water masked (per product name). Aevion exports about 590 m cells with nearest-neighbor sampling, drops cells outside the service's published range, converts cm to m.
provenance.license: NASA data, free to use. Research-grade, not for operational use.

layers.name: Measurement coverage
layers.label: Coverage
layers.hintStory: Bright means the map has solid data around this spot. Dark means there are gaps nearby, so be careful.
layers.hintScientist: Share of valid cells in a 7 by 7 window (about 4 km). Derived by Aevion from the map's gaps. It is not interferometric coherence, which this public map does not include.

provenance.product: Derived by Aevion from the displacement map's valid cells
provenance.method: Mean of the valid-cell mask over a 7 by 7 window
provenance.measurement: Local data completeness, 0 (no valid data nearby) to 1 (fully covered)
